newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OSCE chief says Chechen vote preparations on track.
newsitem.headline: OSCE chief says Chechen vote preparations on track.

text.p: An international mediator trying to help broker a permanent peace settlment in breakaway Chechnya said on Tuesday he was satisfied with the plans for next week's elections despite Russian complaints.

"Given the circumstances, the preparations are going quite well," Tim Guldimann, head of the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe's (OSCE) Chechnya mission, told Reuters in the regional capital Grozny.
"No major problem exists now that could jepoardise their organisation," he said.

Moscow has hinted that it might refuse to recognise the vote unless Chechnya's separatist leaders allow voting stations to be set up in Moscow and other cities for refugees from the 21-month conflict in Chechnya, which ended with a peace deal in August.
The separatists say that most have returned home and that those who remain away can cast ballots on Chechnya's borders.

They say Russia, which withdrew its last troops this month after a failing to crush the separatists in a military campaign launched in December 1994, is looking for an excuse to declare the poll invalid.
Guldimann said the Chechens were making a sincere attempt to help remaining refugees, most of whom are concentrated in Russian regions bordering Chechnya, to be able to vote.

"We see that there are real endeavours on the Chechen side to bring refugees to the republic. They are organising polling stations just across the border. We are assisting them in the financing of this process," he said.

Russia's lower house of parliament, the State Duma, is set to debate a motion on Wednesday reccommending that Guldimann be expelled from Chechnya. He is alleged to have violated the constitution by giving the separatist government money for the election.

The OSCE has so far provided $350,000 to finance everything from ballot boxes to indelible ink skin-stamping devices to prevent double voting. Guldimann said he was unaware of the Duma move and that there was nothing unusual in the monetary aid.

"What we are doing here is helping to facilitate the holding of the election, as we did in Bosnia. Every step of our work has been fully coordinated with the Russian government, including with (Security Council Chairman Ivan) Rybkin. They were informed of everything and supported all of our efforts."
He denied charges that the OSCE did not support Russia's territorial integrity. "The status of Chechnya for the OSCE is very clear. Chechnya is part of the Russian Federation."

Sixteen candidates are effectively vying to succeed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the first president of the self-proclaimed republic elected in 1991 and killed in the 21-month war between his pro- independence forces and thousands of Russian troops.
The former chief of the Chechen guerrilla army, Aslan Maskhadov, is widely viewed as the favorite candidate.

Other frontrunners are former field commander Shamil Basayev, charged with terrorism by Moscow for a bloody 1995 hostage-taking incident, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and wartime propoganda chief Movladi Udugov.
If no candidate gets 50 percent then a second round of voting will be held in three weeks' time.
